claims.claim: The PNCM has built a working strategy around improvements to the surveillance and management system operating nationally through the health facility and community health worker network.
claims.source: To this end, the PNCM has built a working strategy around improvements to the surveillance and management system operating nationally through the health facility and community health worker (CHW) network, and the delivery of information and interventions targeted at sub-national administrative regions hosting identified transmission foci (Boncy et al., 2015; Druetz et al., 2018).
claims.evidence: The claim is supported by citations to Boncy et al., 2015 and Druetz et al., 2018.

claims.claim: The PNCM has collaborated with the Malaria Atlas Project and partners to geo-locate transmission foci and develop evidence-based risk stratification.
claims.source: To precisely geo-locate transmission foci and develop an evidence-based risk stratification, the PNCM has collaborated with the Malaria Atlas Project (MAP) and partners.
claims.evidence: This is a direct statement about the collaboration.

claims.claim: The study constructed a national-level endemicity map and seasonality profile informed by routine case reports from health facilities.
claims.source: In this study, we describe an important component of this collaboration: the construction of a national-level endemicity map and seasonality profile informed by routine case reports from health facilities.
claims.evidence: This is a direct statement of the study's objective and output.

claims.claim: Recent years have seen great progress in the adoption of Bayesian methods for probabilistic map-making among the infectious disease and global health research community.
claims.source: Recent years have seen great progress in the adoption of Bayesian methods for probabilistic map-making (known as model-based geostatistics; Diggle et al., 1998) among the infectious disease and global health research community (Bhatt et al., 2015; Osgood-Zimmerman et al., 2018; Zouré et al., 2014; Karagiannis-Voules et al., 2015).
claims.evidence: The claim is supported by multiple citations to relevant literature.

claims.claim: Model-based geostatistics is an extension to the generalised linear model whereby geographic covariates are combined with a Gaussian process representing spatially correlated residuals.
claims.source: The standard form of this technique is an extension to the generalised linear model whereby geographic covariates based on high-resolution satellite imaging (e.g., land surface temperature; digital elevation; nighttime lights) are combined additively with a Gaussian process representing spatially correlated residuals.
claims.evidence: This is a description of the standard methodology.

claims.claim: Routine case reporting data in sub-Saharan Africa have historically been highly incomplete and/or subject to problematic sources of bias.
claims.source: In the case of malaria, these methods provide benchmark estimates of transmission intensity (World Health Organization, 2019; Weiss et al., 2019; Battle et al., 2019) for much of sub-Saharan Africa where (1) routine case reporting data have historically been highly incomplete and/or subject to problematic sources of bias (Rowe et al., 2009; Alegana et al., 2020)
claims.evidence: The claim is supported by citations to Rowe et al., 2009 and Alegana et al., 2020.

claims.claim: In low transmission settings such as Haiti, transmission typically becomes increasingly focalised.
claims.source: In low transmission settings such as Haiti, transmission typically becomes increasingly focalised, and the low prevalence of patent parasitaemia forces community parasite surveys towards very intensive (viz. expensive) sampling designs to achieve confident spatial stratifications.
claims.evidence: This is a general statement about low transmission settings applied to Haiti.

claims.claim: Low prevalence of patent parasitaemia forces community parasite surveys towards very intensive sampling designs to achieve confident spatial stratifications.
claims.source: In low transmission settings such as Haiti, transmission typically becomes increasingly focalised, and the low prevalence of patent parasitaemia forces community parasite surveys towards very intensive (viz. expensive) sampling designs to achieve confident spatial stratifications.
claims.evidence: This is a logical inference about the requirements for survey design in low prevalence settings.

claims.claim: Spatio-temporal risk modelling from routine passive surveillance data may be a more effective means of describing malaria heterogeneity in low transmission settings than community parasite surveys.
claims.source: Spatio-temporal risk modelling from data deriving from a routine passive surveillance process, such as the reporting of health facility case counts, may thus be a more effective means of describing the heterogeneity of malaria in this setting.
claims.evidence: This is a speculative statement about the potential effectiveness of the approach.

claims.claim: A major challenge in disease mapping from health facility case data is that case counts represent aggregation over an area of unknown extent (the health facility catchment).
claims.source: Foremost of these is that the case count from a given facility represents the aggregation of observable case incidence over all households over an area of unknown extent: the health facility catchment.
claims.evidence: This is a statement about a known methodological challenge.

claims.claim: Extension of the MGB framework requires development of a sophisticated sub-model linking fine-scale disease process with aggregate data.
claims.source: Extension of the MGB framework requires the development of a sophisticated sub-model linking the fine-scale disease process with the aggregate data (Wilson and Wakefield, 2020; Taylor et al., 2018; Sturrock et al., 2014), including a representation of health facility choice and attendance (Duncan et al., 2016; Nelli et al., 2020).
claims.evidence: The claim is supported by multiple citations to relevant methodological literature.

claims.claim: There is a lack of information regarding spatio-temporal variations in treatment seeking propensities across Haitian communities.
claims.source: Further challenges include a lack of information regarding spatio-temporal variations in treatment seeking propensities across the studied communities (Alegana et al., 2017b; Alegana et al., 2012; Battle et al., 2016; Karyana et al., 2016)
claims.evidence: The claim is supported by citations to relevant literature on treatment seeking behavior.

claims.claim: There is a lack of information regarding spatio-temporal variations in diagnostic practices operating at each health facility in Haiti.
claims.source: Further challenges include a lack of information regarding spatio-temporal variations in treatment seeking propensities across the studied communities (Alegana et al., 2017b; Alegana et al., 2012; Battle et al., 2016; Karyana et al., 2016) and in the diagnostic practices operating at each health facility (Bastiaens et al., 2014).
claims.evidence: The claim is supported by a citation to Bastiaens et al., 2014.

claims.claim: Validation of down-scaling models is uniquely challenging because hold-out of aggregate response data is of limited utility for testing fine-scale accuracy.
claims.source: Validation of model outputs from this class of 'down-scaling' models is also uniquely challenging; the hold-out of aggregate response data is of limited utility for testing fine-scale accuracy, since only ancillary point-level observations can overcome the potential for 'ecological fallacy' (Wakefield and Smith, 2016).
claims.evidence: The claim is supported by a citation to Wakefield and Smith, 2016.

claims.claim: Serological tools that quantify immune responses to malaria antigens can reveal whether an individual has ever carried a Plasmodium falciparum parasite infection.
claims.source: For example, serological tools that quantify immune responses to particular malaria antigens can reveal whether or not an individual has ever carried a Pf parasite infection (Corran et al., 2007; Helb et al., 2015)
claims.evidence: The claim is supported by citations to Corran et al., 2007 and Helb et al., 2015.

claims.claim: Serological data targeting lifetime exposure history gain statistical power from lower sampling variance at the expense of temporal precision.
claims.source: serological tools that quantify immune responses to particular malaria antigens can reveal whether or not an individual has ever carried a Pf parasite infection (Corran et al., 2007; Helb et al., 2015), effectively targeting a higher prevalence objective (i.e., lifetime exposure history instead of current infection status) to gain statistical power from lower sampling variance at the expense of temporal precision.
claims.evidence: This is an inference about the statistical properties of serological data.

claims.claim: Serological data have been gathered in Haiti and used to assist with malaria risk stratification.
claims.source: Data of this nature have been gathered in Haiti and used in various ways to assist with malaria risk stratification (Oviedo et al., 2020).
claims.evidence: The claim is supported by a citation to Oviedo et al., 2020.

claims.claim: The study used a geostatistical model informed by routine case incidence reports at monthly cadence from across Haiti over a 6-year period (2014-2019).
claims.source: Here we present the results of a bespoke analysis designed to uncover the characteristic spatial pattern of contemporary malaria endemicity in Haiti and its spatio-temporal seasonality profile using a geostatistical model informed by routine case incidence reports at monthly cadence assembled from across the country over a 6-year period (2014–2019 inclusive).
claims.evidence: This is a direct statement about the study design and data used.

claims.claim: The maps produced have focused the delivery of indoor residual spraying and focal mass drug administration in the Grand'Anse Department in South-Western Haiti.
claims.source: These maps have focussed the delivery of indoor residual spraying and focal mass drug administration in the Grand'Anse Department in South-Western Haiti.
claims.evidence: This is a direct statement about the application of the study outputs.

claims.claim: Large areas of Haiti, particularly in the northern departments of Nord-Ouest, Nord, and Nord-Est, and along the Chaîne de la Selle mountain range, are essentially malaria free with fewer than one in 10,000 individuals expected to experience clinical malaria each year.
claims.source: Large areas of the country – in particular, in the northern departments of Nord-Ouest, Nord, and Nord-Est, and along the Chaîne de la Selle mountain range tracing the border of the Ouest and Sud-Est departments – are essentially malaria free with fewer than one in 10,000 individuals expected to experience clinical malarial each year.
claims.evidence: This is a finding from the model-based analysis presented in the study.

claims.claim: High burden malaria communities in Haiti are located primarily along the coastline and rivers of the Tiburon peninsula containing the Grand'Anse, Sud, and Nippes departments.
claims.source: These high burden communities are located primarily along the coastline and rivers of the Tiburon peninsula containing the Grand'Anse, Sud, and Nippes departments
claims.evidence: This is a finding from the model-based analysis presented in the study.

claims.claim: The population-at-risk in Grand'Anse department is 322,693 (95% CI: 280,707–372,057).
claims.source: These high burden communities are located primarily along the coastline and rivers of the Tiburon peninsula containing the Grand'Anse, Sud, and Nippes departments, with populations-at-risk (defined as those living in an area of malaria incidence greater than one case per 1000 PYO) of 322,693 (95% CI: 280,707–372,057), 322,956 (95% CI: 202,462–392,047), and 108,077 (95% CI: 61,620–147,288), respectively.
claims.evidence: This is a quantitative finding from the model-based analysis.

claims.claim: The population-at-risk in Sud department is 322,956 (95% CI: 202,462–392,047).
claims.source: These high burden communities are located primarily along the coastline and rivers of the Tiburon peninsula containing the Grand'Anse, Sud, and Nippes departments, with populations-at-risk (defined as those living in an area of malaria incidence greater than one case per 1000 PYO) of 322,693 (95% CI: 280,707–372,057), 322,956 (95% CI: 202,462–392,047), and 108,077 (95% CI: 61,620–147,288), respectively.
claims.evidence: This is a quantitative finding from the model-based analysis.

claims.claim: The population-at-risk in Nippes department is 108,077 (95% CI: 61,620–147,288).
claims.source: These high burden communities are located primarily along the coastline and rivers of the Tiburon peninsula containing the Grand'Anse, Sud, and Nippes departments, with populations-at-risk (defined as those living in an area of malaria incidence greater than one case per 1000 PYO) of 322,693 (95% CI: 280,707–372,057), 322,956 (95% CI: 202,462–392,047), and 108,077 (95% CI: 61,620–147,288), respectively.
claims.evidence: This is a quantitative finding from the model-based analysis.

claims.claim: An additional area of lower but substantial malaria burden lies within the central river valley joining the Artibonite and Centre departments.
claims.source: An additional area of lower but still substantial burden lies within the central river valley joining the Artibonite and Centre departments, with populations-at-risk of 174,766 (95% CI: 97,196–313,169) and 166,938 (95% CI: 95,070–281,816).
claims.evidence: This is a finding from the model-based analysis.

claims.claim: The population-at-risk in Artibonite department is 174,766 (95% CI: 97,196–313,169).
claims.source: An additional area of lower but still substantial burden lies within the central river valley joining the Artibonite and Centre departments, with populations-at-risk of 174,766 (95% CI: 97,196–313,169) and 166,938 (95% CI: 95,070–281,816).
claims.evidence: This is a quantitative finding from the model-based analysis.

claims.claim: The population-at-risk in Centre department is 166,938 (95% CI: 95,070–281,816).
claims.source: An additional area of lower but still substantial burden lies within the central river valley joining the Artibonite and Centre departments, with populations-at-risk of 174,766 (95% CI: 97,196–313,169) and 166,938 (95% CI: 95,070–281,816).
claims.evidence: This is a quantitative finding from the model-based analysis.

claims.claim: The broad credible intervals around population-at-risk estimates reflect systematic uncertainties of the de-trending, RDT-standardising, and imputation component of the model.
claims.source: The broad credible intervals around the estimation of these populations-at-risk reflect in large part the systematic uncertainties of the de-trending, RDT-standardising, and imputation component of our model, which contribute a substantial variance to inference of the absolute clinical incidence rate, but less so to its relative spatial distribution.
claims.evidence: This is an interpretation of the model uncertainty by the authors.

claims.claim: Regions of particularly high variance in the uncertainty summary correspond to the Chaîne de la Selle mountain range and patches along the borders of the Artibonite department and in Nord and Nord-Ouest departments.
claims.source: Inspection of the uncertainty summary in Figure 1C indicates regions of particularly high variance corresponding to (1) the Chaîne de la Selle mountain range and (2) patches along the borders of the Artibonite department and in Nord and Nord-Ouest departments.
claims.evidence: This is a finding from inspection of Figure 1C.

claims.claim: High variance in the Chaîne de la Selle mountain range is explained by population sparsity combined with extreme elevation.
claims.source: The explanation for the former is simply population sparsity (i.e., sampling noise) combined with the extreme elevation (i.e., covariate slope uncertainty)
claims.evidence: This is an interpretation provided by the authors.

claims.claim: The Chaîne de la Selle mountain range is probably well-classified as low malaria risk because it is believed to be an unlikely habitat for Anopheles albimanus.
claims.source: however, since this terrain is believed to be an unlikely habitat for the local Anopheles species (principally A. albimanus) (Frederick et al., 2016), it is probably well-classified as low risk.
claims.evidence: This is an inference based on knowledge about vector habitat preferences, supported by citation to Frederick et al., 2016.

claims.claim: High variance in patches along the borders of Artibonite and in Nord and Nord-Ouest departments is explained by ongoing use of microscopic diagnosis at similar frequency to RDT diagnosis at a minority of health facilities.
claims.source: The explanation for the latter is the ongoing use of microscopic diagnosis at similar frequency to RDT diagnosis at a minority of health facilities in these areas (most used RDT diagnosis near-exclusively in 2019), which leads to a higher contribution here from uncertainty in our standardisation procedure.
claims.evidence: This is an interpretation provided by the authors based on the data characteristics.

claims.claim: The accuracy of microscopic diagnosis in Haiti has been characterized as inadequate.
claims.source: The accuracy of microscopic diagnosis in Haiti has previously been characterised as inadequate (Landman et al., 2015; Weppelmann et al., 2018), hence the importance of attempting to adjust statistically for diagnostic type.
claims.evidence: The claim is supported by citations to Landman et al., 2015 and Weppelmann et al., 2018.

claims.claim: The estimation of fine-scale spatial patterns below the extent of health facility catchments is driven by the suite of ancillary environmental covariates.
claims.source: The estimation of fine-scale spatial patterns below the extent of health facility catchments is driven within our model by the suite of ancillary environmental covariates.
claims.evidence: This is a statement about the model structure and how it achieves fine-scale predictions.

claims.claim: The most important covariates for annual malaria incidence rate are elevation, accessibility, road presence/absence, and potential evapotranspiration.
claims.source: It is interesting to note that of the four most important covariates over the entire country, three are 'topological' in nature – elevation, accessibility, and road presence/absence – and only one is climatic (potential evapotranspiration).
claims.evidence: This is a finding from the model analysis, as illustrated in Figure 4.

claims.claim: The covariate importance results should not be interpreted as indicative of importance in a causal sense.
claims.source: However, it is essential not to interpret these results as indicative of importance in a causal sense; Figure 4 is presented purely to provide insight into the structure of the fitted regression model.
claims.evidence: This is a cautionary statement by the authors about interpretation of their results.

claims.claim: A method for ranking variables in a causal framework applied to malaria case count data from Madagascar showed results very different from regression-based variable selection.
claims.source: A method for ranking variables in a causal framework has recently been applied to the modelling of malaria case count data from health facilities in Madagascar and the results were shown to be very different to a regression-based variable selection method (Arambepola et al., 2020).
claims.evidence: The claim is supported by a citation to Arambepola et al., 2020.

claims.claim: The spatially varying slope parameter fitted to each covariate may change sign in different parts of the country under the modelling framework.
claims.source: Note also that the spatially varying slope parameter fitted to each covariate may even change sign in different parts of the country under our modelling framework.
claims.evidence: This is a statement about the model structure and its flexibility.

claims.claim: In Grand'Anse, a positive slope is assigned to elevation to penalize high elevations in the Chaîne de la Selle mountain range, while a negative slope is assigned to boost predicted incidence along the low-lying coastal fringe.
claims.source: For instance, a positive slope is assigned to penalise high elevations in the Chaîne de la Selle mountain range of the Ouest and Sud-Est departments, while in Grand'Anse, a negative slope is assigned to boost the predicted incidence along the (low-lying) coastal fringe.
claims.evidence: This is a description of how the model assigns different relationships in different regions.

claims.claim: The catchment model allows patients in any location to split their attendance between multiple neighbouring facilities according to relative travel time and a relative attractiveness weight.
claims.source: The structure of the catchment model used here (see the Materials and methods section for details) allows for patients in any given location to split their attendance between multiple neighbouring facilities according to the relative travel time to each (fixed input) and a relative attractiveness weight (free parameter learnt during fitting).
claims.evidence: This is a description of the catchment model structure.

claims.claim: The resulting catchments may have overlapping boundaries, which avoids unrealistic structural effects.
claims.source: The resulting catchments may thus have overlapping boundaries, which avoids unrealistic structural effects – such as a systematic under-estimation of city health facility patient populations when commuters may otherwise be erroneously assigned to exclusively visit suburban facilities – but can be a challenge for visualisation.
claims.evidence: This is a statement about the advantages and challenges of the model structure.

claims.claim: The dominant seasonal signal is a uniphasic seasonal profile evident across most of Haiti, with cases rising during October-November to a peak in December-January and declining rapidly from February to a low during April-May.
claims.source: The dominant signal is a uniphasic seasonal profile evident across most of the country, and most notably the central valley, with cases rising during October–November to a peak in December–January and then declining rapidly from February to a low during April–May.
claims.evidence: This is a finding from the spatio-temporal model analysis, as illustrated in Figure 6.

claims.claim: A small number of locations, notably one hotspot on the northern coast of Grand'Anse near Jeremie, show a tentative suggestion of a biphasic character with a smaller second peak in June.
claims.source: A small number of locations – notably one hotspot on the northern coast of Grand'Anse near the town of Jeremie – show a tentative suggestion of a biphasic character with a smaller, second peak in June.
claims.evidence: This is a finding from the spatio-temporal model analysis.

claims.claim: The biphasic pattern near Jeremie may be an artefact of a recent epidemic outbreak that has not been entirely resolved by the cleaning and imputation procedure.
claims.source: However, it is possible that this is an artefact of the recent epidemic outbreak in this area that has not been entirely resolved by our cleaning and imputation procedure for constructing a dataset of representative (endemic character) case counts.
claims.evidence: This is a speculative statement by the authors about a potential limitation.

claims.claim: In high incidence areas of the central valley and Grand'Anse, the most important positive covariate is the enhanced vegetation index lagged by 2 months.
claims.source: In the high incidence areas of the central valley and the Grand'Anse, the most important positive covariate in a predictive sense is the enhanced vegetation index (EVI) lagged by 2 months
claims.evidence: This is a finding from the spatio-temporal model analysis, as illustrated in Figure 7.

claims.claim: In the central valley, the most important negative covariate is land surface temperature lagged by 1 month.
claims.source: while the most important negative covariate is the land surface temperature (LST) lagged by 1 month in the former
claims.evidence: This is a finding from the spatio-temporal model analysis, as illustrated in Figure 7.

claims.claim: In Grand'Anse, the most important negative covariate is the enhanced vegetation index unlagged.
claims.source: and the EVI unlagged in the latter
claims.evidence: This is a finding from the spatio-temporal model analysis, as illustrated in Figure 7.

claims.claim: The fitted model covariates should not be directly interpreted as physical drivers of malaria incidence because the model is designed from a predictive framework rather than one of causal inference.
claims.source: Again, note that although these covariates may plausibly reflect physical drivers of malaria incidence in Haiti, we caution against this direct interpretation as the fitted model is designed from a predictive framework rather than one of causal inference.
claims.evidence: This is a cautionary statement by the authors about interpretation.

claims.claim: All climatic and vegetation cover covariates are highly co-linear.
claims.source: Moreover, all of these climatic and vegetation cover covariates are themselves highly co-linear, so upon exclusion of one there is typically another able to be identified as providing an explanatory contribution of similar magnitude within the regression model.
claims.evidence: This is a statement about the statistical properties of the covariates.

claims.claim: The TAS program used serological markers of long-term malaria exposure (AMA and MSP antigenic responses) to characterize malaria endemicity in school-aged children.
claims.source: The TAS program used serological markers of long-term malaria exposure – apical membrane antigen (AMA) and merozoite surface protein (MSP) antigenic responses – to characterise malaria endemicity in school-aged children.
claims.evidence: This is a description of the TAS program methodology.

claims.claim: The median-to-median correlation between TAS sero-prevalence and predicted clinical incidence rate has a Pearson coefficient of 0.426 (95% CI: 0.353–0.499).
claims.source: The median-to-median correlation between these two metrics of transmission intensity has a Pearson coefficient of 0.426 (95% CI: 0.353–0.499), reflecting a positive but noisy relationship.
claims.evidence: This is a quantitative validation result from comparing model predictions to TAS data.

claims.claim: Much of the width in the scatter plot between TAS sero-prevalence and predicted incidence derives from random sampling noise.
claims.source: Of course, since the TAS sample size per school is generally small (<30), the credible intervals around these point estimates of sero-prevalence are correspondingly broad. When considered in addition to the uncertainties surrounding the fine-scale predictions from our health facility-based model, it is likely that much of the width in this scatter plot derives from random (sampling) noise.
claims.evidence: This is an inference about the sources of uncertainty in the validation comparison.

claims.claim: There is a discrepancy between moderate to high sero-prevalence schools in the Nord department and low predicted clinical incidence rate from the health facility dataset.
claims.source: Where visual comparison of Figure 8A to Figure 1A indicates the most interesting discrepancy is with regard to the presence of some moderate (and in one case, high) sero-prevalence schools in the Nord department for which our predicted clinical incidence rate from the health facility dataset is everywhere rather low.
claims.evidence: This is an observation from comparing Figure 8A to Figure 1A.

claims.claim: The discrepancy in Nord department is suspected to reflect a strong decline in transmission intensity over the period 2014-2016.
claims.source: We suspect that this is a reflection of a strong decline in transmission intensity in this region over the period 2014–2016, seen in the rapid decline in cases reported and hence the strong de-trending in our model towards the 2019 case counts
claims.evidence: This is a speculative interpretation by the authors.

claims.claim: It is not possible to unambiguously distinguish changes to the health reporting system from genuine transmission intensity trends from the available data.
claims.source: although it is not possible to unambiguously distinguish changes to the health reporting system from genuine transmission intensity trends from the available data.
claims.evidence: This is a statement about a limitation of the data.

claims.claim: The incidence surfaces should be understood as reflecting the current state of transmission subject to recent history of anti-malarial interventions, rather than inherent environmental receptivity under a zero intervention scenario.
claims.source: An important point raised by this comparison is that the incidence surfaces presented here should be understood as reflecting the current state of transmission subject to the recent history of anti-malarial interventions, rather than as a reflection of the inherent environmental receptivity under a zero intervention scenario.
claims.evidence: This is an important interpretive caveat provided by the authors.

claims.claim: A minimal alternative approach using naïve imputation and naïve catchment structure yields a correlation coefficient of 0.301 (95% CI: 0.215–0.369) against TAS sero-prevalence data.
claims.source: The correlation coefficient of this risk map against the TAS sero-prevalence data is just 0.301 (95% CI: 0.215–0.369), compared against 0.426 (95% CI: 0.353–0.499) for our preferred model.
claims.evidence: This is a quantitative comparison showing the preferred model performs better.

claims.claim: Using de-trending, imputing, and diagnostic correcting on the naïve catchment model improves the correlation against TAS sero-prevalences to 0.331 (95% CI: 0.257–0.398).
claims.source: A second version of the naïve catchment risk map is shown in Figure 9B, this time after using our Step one and Step two models (see Materials and methods) for de-trending, imputing, and diagnostic correcting the raw case data. Overall, this adjustment improves the correlation against the TAS sero-prevalences to 0.331 (95% CI: 0.257–0.398).
claims.evidence: This is a quantitative comparison showing the value of the data processing steps.

claims.claim: The naïve approach would suggest that transmission in Grand'Anse is dominated by hotspots sharply concentrated on the townships of Abricots, Bonbon, Anse-d'Hainault, and Les Irois with transmission intensity above 100 cases per 1000 PYO in each.
claims.source: Compared with our preferred model-based risk map (Figure 1), the result here would suggest that transmission in the Grand'Anse is dominated by hotspots sharply concentrated on the townships of Abricots, Bonbon, Anse-d'Hainault, and Les Irois, with transmission intensity above 100 cases per 1000 PYO in each, rather than being spread more evenly throughout the coastal settlements and rural communities of this peninsula.
claims.evidence: This is a comparison of the naïve approach results to the preferred model.

claims.claim: The fine-scale mapping brings a greatly refined understanding of the elimination challenge in Haiti.
claims.source: The fine-scale mapping of malaria incidence and its seasonality profile in Haiti achieved through our fitting of a Bayesian geospatial regression framework with catchment sub-model to the 2014–2019 health facility case reports brings a greatly refined understanding of the elimination challenge on this side of Hispaniola.
claims.evidence: This is a summary statement about the value of the study.

claims.claim: Communities suffering from the highest annual average rates of clinical malaria (above 50 cases per 1000 PYO) in 2019 are those along the coastline and valleys of the Grand'Anse and Sud departments.
claims.source: We see that the communities suffering from the highest annual average rates of clinical malaria (above 50 cases per 1000 PYO) in 2019 are those along the coastline and valleys of the Grand'Anse and Sud departments.
claims.evidence: This is a summary finding from the model analysis.

claims.claim: Additional pockets of low-to-moderate endemicity (1-10 cases per 1000 PYO) are located in the central valley spanning Artibonite and Centre departments, in some coastal communities of Nippes, Sud-Est, and Nord-Est departments, and surrounding Port-au-Prince in Ouest department.
claims.source: Additional pockets of low-to-moderate endemicity (1–10 cases per 1000 PYO) are located in the central valley spanning the Artibonite and Centre departments, in some coastal communities of the Nippes, Sud-Est, and Nord-Est departments, and surrounding Port-au-Prince in the Ouest department
claims.evidence: This is a summary finding from the model analysis.

claims.claim: The area surrounding Port-au-Prince accounts for a substantial proportion of total cases each year owing to the size of the population.
claims.source: the latter accounting for a substantial proportion of the total cases each year owing to the size of the population in this area.
claims.evidence: This is an inference based on the combination of incidence rates and population density.

claims.claim: The Nord and Nord-Est departments have lower incidence rates (below 1 case per 1000 PYO), and some areas can be confidently predicted as extremely low (below 1 case per 10,000 PYO).
claims.source: The Nord and Nord-Est departments have lower incidence rates (below 1 case per 1000 PYO), and some areas can yet be confidently predicted as extremely low (below 1 case per 10,000 PYO).
claims.evidence: This is a summary finding from the model analysis.

claims.claim: There exists substantial heterogeneity in the clinical incidence rate of malaria at small scales within departments.
claims.source: Against these broad variations between departments, there exists substantial heterogeneity in the clinical incidence rate of malaria at rather small scales within departments
claims.evidence: This is a summary finding from the model analysis.

claims.claim: In a predictive sense, heterogeneity within departments can be explained by differences in accessibility, elevation, road presence/absence, and potential evapotranspiration.
claims.source: which in a predictive sense can be explained within our modelling approach by differences in accessibility, elevation, road presence/absence, and potential evapotranspiration.
claims.evidence: This is a summary of the model's covariate findings.

claims.claim: The clinical incidence of malaria in Haiti is highly seasonal with a strong uniphasic seasonality pattern at maximum during December-January and minimum during April-May.
claims.source: The clinical incidence of malaria in Haiti is also highly seasonal with a strong uniphasic seasonality pattern at maximum during December–January and minimum during April–May.
claims.evidence: This is a summary finding from the spatio-temporal model analysis.

claims.claim: The maps have been used to derive epidemiologically relevant operational units for targeting packages of interventions in five priority communes in Grand'Anse.
claims.source: These maps have been used to derive epidemiologically relevant operational units for targeting packages of interventions in five priority communes in Grand'Anse.
claims.evidence: This is a statement about the application of the study outputs.

claims.claim: Operational units were ranked by the strength of transmission (quantified in terms of the reproduction number under control, Rc) to help determine those that would receive targeted mass drug administration and IRS in 2018.
claims.source: Operational units were ranked by the strength of transmission (quantified after further post-processing in terms of the reproduction number under control, Rc) to help determine those that would receive targeted mass drug administration (tMDA) and with IRS in 2018, and are again being used in planning this year (2020).
claims.evidence: This is a statement about the application of the study outputs.

claims.claim: Serological data were subsequently used to refine the ordering of operational units.
claims.source: Serological data were subsequently used to refine this ordering, and an eventual re-definition of operational unit boundaries was made to follow natural logistical divisions such as rivers and major roads.
claims.evidence: This is a statement about how additional data were used in planning.

claims.claim: Fine-scale probabilistic maps offer a more nuanced stratification than categorical risk maps at the commune level produced by direct summary of case counts divided by areal population totals.

claims.claim: The model was fitted using monthly case counts from 771 health facilities reporting from across Haiti throughout the 6-year period from January 2014 to December 2019.
claims.source: Here we present a key piece of this planning: an up-to-date, fine-scale endemicity map and seasonality profile for Haiti informed by monthly case counts from 771 health facilities reporting from across the country throughout the 6-year period from January 2014 to December 2019.
claims.evidence: This is a description of the data used from the abstract.

results.result: The study addresses malaria elimination in Haiti, a low-transmission setting where Plasmodium falciparum prevalence is below 1% in many areas and the dominant vector Anopheles albimanus is inefficient. The National Malaria Control Program (PNCM) has prioritized elimination and collaborated with the Malaria Atlas Project to construct a national-level endemicity map and seasonality profile using routine health facility case reports.
results.evaluation: Claims C1-C8 establish the epidemiological context and study objectives. The claims are well-supported by appropriate citations to WHO reports, peer-reviewed literature on vector biology, and descriptions of the PNCM's strategic approach. These contextual claims provide necessary background for understanding the study's rationale.

results.result: The study used monthly malaria case counts from 771 health facilities reporting at least once in 2019 (a subset of 1,191 facilities), covering January 2014 to December 2019 with 77.5% reporting completeness. After imputation and aggregation, 450 'aggregate pseudo-facilities' were formed. High-resolution satellite covariates, population data from Facebook's High Resolution Settlement Layer, and travel-time maps were incorporated. Serological data from 24,514 children in 820 schools (TAS dataset, 2014-2016) were used for validation.
results.evaluation: Claims C23, C104-C114 describe the primary data sources and are well-documented with specific quantitative details. The data processing steps (aggregation, imputation) are clearly stated. The use of multiple data types (case counts, covariates, serological validation data) is appropriate for the modeling framework. Data completeness metrics provide transparency about data quality.

results.result: A novel three-stage hierarchical Bayesian modeling framework was developed to map malaria incidence from health facility data. Stage 1 imputes missing data and de-trends case counts toward RDT-standardized 2019 levels. Stage 2 fits a spatial-only geostatistical model with flexible catchment sub-model to estimate annual incidence and facility attractiveness. Stage 3 fits a spatio-temporal model conditional on the catchment to explain seasonal variation. Modularization guards against error magnification between components.
results.evaluation: Claims C115-C120, C122 describe the methodological framework. The three-stage approach is clearly articulated with appropriate justification for modularization (computational feasibility, focus on endemic transmission, error containment). The hierarchical Bayesian structure is standard for geostatistical modeling. Citations to relevant methodological literature (Plummer 2015, Jacob 2017) support the approach. The novelty claim regarding the catchment sub-model appears reasonable given the complexity described.

results.result: The model reveals extreme spatial heterogeneity in malaria incidence across Haiti. Large areas in northern departments (Nord-Ouest, Nord, Nord-Est) and the Chaîne de la Selle mountain range have very low incidence (<1 per 10,000 PYO). High-burden communities (>50 cases per 1,000 PYO) are concentrated along the coastline and rivers of the Tiburon peninsula (Grand'Anse, Sud, Nippes departments) with populations-at-risk of 322,693, 322,956, and 108,077 respectively. Additional moderate-burden areas exist in the central valley (Artibonite and Centre departments) with populations-at-risk of 174,766 and 166,938, and around Port-au-Prince.
results.evaluation: Claims C25-C32, C67-C71 present the main spatial findings with specific quantitative estimates and confidence intervals. The geographic patterns are consistent with the visual evidence in Figures 1-3. The population-at-risk estimates include appropriate uncertainty quantification (95% CIs). The identification of high-burden areas in Grand'Anse and moderate-burden areas in the central valley is clearly supported by the model outputs. The finding of substantial small-scale heterogeneity within departments is a key result.

results.result: Broad credible intervals around population-at-risk estimates reflect systematic uncertainties from de-trending, RDT-standardization, and imputation. High variance regions correspond to the Chaîne de la Selle mountain range (explained by population sparsity and extreme elevation, but likely correctly classified as low risk due to unsuitable vector habitat) and patches in Artibonite, Nord, and Nord-Ouest (explained by ongoing microscopy use at some facilities, which has been characterized as inadequate in Haiti).
results.evaluation: Claims C33-C38 provide important interpretation of model uncertainties. The explanations for high-variance regions are reasonable and supported by citations (Frederick et al. 2016 for vector habitat; Landman et al. 2015, Weppelmann et al. 2018 for microscopy accuracy). The acknowledgment of systematic uncertainties from data processing steps demonstrates appropriate scientific caution. The inference about the Chaîne de la Selle being correctly classified despite high uncertainty is justified by ecological reasoning.

results.result: Fine-scale spatial patterns below health facility catchment extent are driven by environmental covariates. The most important covariates are elevation, accessibility, road presence/absence, and potential evapotranspiration (three topological, one climatic). However, these should not be interpreted causally—they reflect the fitted regression structure. The spatially varying slope parameters can change sign across regions (e.g., elevation has opposite effects in different departments).
results.evaluation: Claims C39-C44 describe covariate importance findings with appropriate caveats. The identification of topological covariates as dominant is interesting and supported by Figure 4. The authors correctly caution against causal interpretation (C41, C53), citing Arambepola et al. 2020 showing differences between regression-based and causal variable selection. The spatially varying coefficient structure (C43-C44) is a strength of the modeling approach, allowing relationships to differ geographically. The example of elevation having opposite effects in different regions is well-explained.

results.result: The catchment model allows patients to split attendance between multiple facilities based on travel time and learned attractiveness weights, resulting in overlapping catchments. This gravity-style representation is more sophisticated than Euclidean distances or hard boundaries, though still a simplification. Almost 96.4% of populated pixels lie within 100 minutes travel time from their nearest facility. Validation against TAS serological data suggests the model is on the right track for downscaling.
results.evaluation: Claims C45-C46, C89-C91, C121 describe the catchment sub-model, a key methodological innovation. The overlapping catchment structure is more realistic than hard boundaries and is well-justified. The quantitative finding about accessibility (C121) is important for understanding treatment-seeking behavior. The acknowledgment that the model is still a simplification (C90) demonstrates appropriate scientific humility. The validation statement (C91) is supported by the correlation results with TAS data (C56, C63-C64).

results.result: Malaria incidence in Haiti exhibits strong uniphasic seasonality, peaking in December-January and reaching a low in April-May. A small number of locations (notably near Jeremie in Grand'Anse) show tentative biphasic patterns with a second peak in June, possibly an artifact of epidemic outbreaks. In high-incidence areas, the most important positive covariate is EVI lagged 2 months; the most important negative covariates are LST lagged 1 month (central valley) and unlagged EVI (Grand'Anse). These should not be interpreted as causal drivers, and climatic/vegetation covariates are highly collinear.
results.evaluation: Claims C47-C54, C73 present the seasonality findings. The dominant uniphasic pattern is clearly shown in Figure 6 and is a major result. The tentative biphasic pattern near Jeremie is appropriately qualified as uncertain (C48-C49). The covariate findings (C50-C52) are supported by Figure 7. The caveats about causal interpretation (C53) and collinearity (C54) are important and demonstrate appropriate statistical reasoning. The seasonality profile has clear programmatic implications for timing interventions.

results.result: Validation against TAS serological data (AMA/MSP responses in school-aged children) shows a Pearson correlation of 0.426 (95% CI: 0.353-0.499) between sero-prevalence and predicted incidence. Much of the scatter likely derives from sampling noise. A discrepancy exists in Nord department where moderate-to-high sero-prevalence schools contrast with low predicted incidence, possibly reflecting transmission decline during 2014-2016, though changes in reporting cannot be distinguished from genuine trends. The incidence surfaces reflect current transmission under recent interventions, not inherent environmental receptivity.
results.evaluation: Claims C55-C62 present the validation results. The correlation coefficient of 0.426 indicates moderate agreement between two independent data sources measuring different aspects of transmission (current incidence vs. lifetime exposure). The explanation for scatter (C57) is reasonable given small TAS sample sizes. The Nord department discrepancy (C59-C61) is honestly reported and the proposed explanation (transmission decline) is plausible. The important caveat (C62) that maps reflect current transmission under interventions rather than baseline receptivity is crucial for interpretation.

results.result: A minimal alternative approach using naïve imputation and naïve catchment structure yields correlation of 0.301 (95% CI: 0.215-0.369) against TAS data, compared to 0.426 for the preferred model. Adding de-trending, imputation, and diagnostic correction improves this to 0.331 (95% CI: 0.257-0.398). The naïve approach suggests transmission in Grand'Anse is concentrated in sharp hotspots (>100 cases per 1,000 PYO) rather than spread more evenly.
results.evaluation: Claims C63-C65 provide important comparative validation showing the value of the sophisticated modeling approach. The preferred model shows substantially better correlation with validation data (0.426 vs 0.301), with non-overlapping confidence intervals. The incremental improvement from data processing steps (0.301 to 0.331) and from the full model (0.331 to 0.426) demonstrates the value of both components. The comparison of spatial patterns (C65) illustrates how the naïve approach produces unrealistic sharp hotspots. This is strong evidence supporting the methodological choices.

results.result: The maps have been used operationally to focus IRS and focal mass drug administration in Grand'Anse, derive epidemiologically relevant operational units in five priority communes, and rank areas by transmission strength (Rc) to determine intervention targeting in 2018 and 2020. Fine-scale probabilistic maps offer more nuanced stratification than commune-level categorical maps or elevation-based dichotomous maps. Point-of-care case counts can generate programmatically useful maps providing fine-scale risk stratifications and seasonality profiles for targeting interventions. Outputs are readily updatable and will be valuable for defining residual transmission foci as elimination nears.
results.evaluation: Claims C24, C74-C78, C99-C103 describe the operational impact and programmatic value of the work. The actual use of maps for intervention planning in Grand'Anse (C24, C74-C76) demonstrates real-world impact. The comparative statements about superiority over simpler approaches (C77-C78) are supported by the validation results. The conclusions about utility (C99-C101) are justified by the demonstrated applications. The statements about updatability (C102) and future value (C103) are reasonable projections. This represents successful translation of research to public health practice.

results.result: Important limitations include lack of information on spatial variations in treatment-seeking behavior (some Haitians seek care outside the national system). The study adjusted for travel-time effects using a model from an African setting, which requires refinement with local data. Seasonal migration and human movement are not explicitly modeled due to lack of high-fidelity movement data for Haiti, though Port-au-Prince appears strongly connected to other departments. The model maps where people at risk reside, not necessarily where infections were contracted. Substantial cases occur around Port-au-Prince, but the role of local transmission vs. importation is unclear.
results.evaluation: Claims C79-C88 provide honest assessment of important limitations. The lack of treatment-seeking data (C79-C81) is a significant gap, and the use of an African-calibrated model is appropriately flagged as requiring local validation. The inability to model human movement (C82-C84) is a real limitation, though the authors reasonably note that high-risk areas are primarily rural where long-distance commuting is unlikely (C86). The distinction between residence and infection location (C85, C88) is an important conceptual point. The acknowledgment of these limitations strengthens rather than weakens the paper by demonstrating scientific rigor.

results.result: Ongoing and future work includes: (1) exploring more complex catchment sub-models in Artibonite using case tracing data, which reveals patients sometimes travel far beyond nearest facilities (possibly to avoid illegal charges); (2) incorporating serological data beyond validation to refine risk maps; (3) developing methods for simultaneous modeling of multiple data types (point and areal data, multiple disease metrics), which is an active research area; and (4) further refinement of Grand'Anse incidence maps using multiple data types.
results.evaluation: Claims C92-C98 describe ongoing research directions. The case tracing work in Artibonite (C92-C94) addresses catchment model limitations with empirical data. The finding that patients sometimes bypass nearby facilities (C93) is important for understanding healthcare-seeking behavior. The proposed integration of serological data (C95-C96) and multiple data types (C97-C98) represents logical extensions supported by appropriate citations. These future directions are well-motivated by the current study's limitations and findings.

results.result: The study is situated within the broader context of model-based geostatistics for disease mapping. In low-transmission settings like Haiti, transmission becomes focalized and low prevalence forces intensive survey designs. Routine passive surveillance may be more effective than community surveys for describing heterogeneity. Challenges include unknown catchment extents, lack of information on treatment-seeking and diagnostic practices, and validation difficulties. Serological tools offer an alternative by targeting lifetime exposure with lower sampling variance but reduced temporal precision.
